candidate_rows.text:
### Static elements

Since version 1.16.0, cached functions can contain Streamlit commands! For example, you can do this:

```python
@st.cache_data
def get_api_data():
    data = api.get(...)
    st.success("Fetched data from API!")  # 👈 Show a success message
    return data
```

As we know, Streamlit only runs this function if it hasn’t been cached before. On this first run, the `st.success` message will appear in the app. But what happens on subsequent runs? It still shows up! Streamlit realizes that there is an `st.` command inside the cached function, saves it during the first run, and replays it on subsequent runs. Replaying static elements works for both caching decorators.

You can also use this functionality to cache entire parts of your UI:

```python
@st.cache_data
def show_data():
    st.header("Data analysis")
    data = api.get(...)
    st.success("Fetched data from API!")
    st.write("Here is a plot of the data:")
    st.line_chart(data)
    st.write("And here is the raw data:")
    st.dataframe(data)
```

candidate_rows.title: Deduplicate identical `st.cache_data` return values to save memory
candidate_rows.text:
### Summary

`st.cache_data` stores one serialized (pickled) blob per cache key, where the key is derived only from the function + input arguments. If a function returns the *same* value (e.g. the same dataframe) for many different inputs, each of those cache entries stores a full, redundant copy. We could recognize identical serialized return values (e.g. by hashing the serialized value bytes) and store the payload only once, with each cache key referencing it — saving memory (and disk when persisted).

Decorator to cache functions that return global resources (e.g. database connections, ML models).

Cached objects are shared across all users, sessions, and reruns. They
must be thread-safe because they can be accessed from multiple threads
concurrently. If thread safety is an issue, consider using ``st.session_state``
to store resources per session instead.

cache with ``st.cache_resource.clear()``.

unhashable argument (like a database connection) or an argument you
want to exclude from caching, use an underscore prefix in the argument
name. In this case, Streamlit will return a cached value when all other
arguments match a previous function call. Alternatively, you can
declare custom hashing functions with ``hash_funcs``.

Cached values are available to all users of your app. If you need to
save results that should only be accessible within a session, use
`Session State
<https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/session-state>`_
instead. Within each user session, an ``@st.cache_resource``-decorated
function returns the cached instance of the return value (if the value
is already cached). Therefore, objects cached by ``st.cache_resource``
act like singletons and can mutate. To cache data and return copies,
use ``st.cache_data`` instead. To learn more about caching, see
`Caching overview
<https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/concepts/architecture/caching>`_.

## `st.Page` and `st.navigation`

If you want maximum flexibility in defining your multipage app, we recommend using `st.Page` and `st.navigation`. With `st.Page` you can declare any Python file or `Callable` as a page in your app. Furthermore, you can define common elements for your pages in your entrypoint file (the file you pass to `streamlit run`). With these methods, your entrypoint file becomes like a picture frame shared by all your pages.

You must include `st.navigation` in your entrypoint file to configure your app's navigation menu. This is also how your entrypoint file serves as the router between your pages.

## `st.Page` and `st.navigation`

If you want maximum flexibility in defining your multipage app, we recommend using `st.Page` and `st.navigation`. With `st.Page` you can declare any Python file or `Callable` as a page in your app. Furthermore, you can define common elements for your pages in your entrypoint file (the file you pass to `streamlit run`). With these methods, your entrypoint file becomes like a picture frame shared by all your pages.

You must include `st.navigation` in your entrypoint file to configure your app's navigation menu. This is also how your entrypoint file serves as the router between your pages.

candidate_rows.title: Minimize `StreamlitDuplicateElementId` errors
candidate_rows.text:
**Important caution — be conservative about what goes into ID generation.** Adding container context to the ID changes element identity, which has a subtle downside: a widget that **dynamically moves between containers** (e.g. its wrapping container changes across reruns) would get a new ID and thus lose its identity and state. This is the main risk to weigh (more so than existing widget state resetting on upgrade), and it can be fixed by explicitly setting a `key` on that element so its identity no longer depends on the container context. In particular:
- **Do not** include user-facing **labels/titles** of wrapping containers (e.g. expander label, dialog title, popover label, tab name) in the ID — these change often and would be fragile/surprising. Prefer **explicitly set keys** for disambiguation instead.
- Auto-added context must apply **only to widgets without an explicit `key`**. When a user sets an explicit `key="x"`, the ID must **not** include the added container context — an explicit key should always behave predictably and stay stable regardless of the surrounding containers. Think through backwards compatibility / migration carefully.

candidate_rows.title: Selectbox dropdown renders behind st.dialog (options hidden, mouse clicks don't register)
candidate_rows.text:
### Current Behavior

The dropdown is painted **behind** the dialog, so the options are hidden, and mouse clicks land on the dialog's other widgets instead of the options. The selection does not change. Selecting with the keyboard (Arrow keys + Enter) does work.

Root cause is a stacking-order/z-index mismatch:

- The dropdown `[data-testid="stSelectboxVirtualDropdown"]` is portaled to `<body>` with `z-index: 100000`.
- `st.dialog` (`[data-testid="stDialog"]`) renders at `z-index: 1000060`.

Because the dialog's z-index is higher, it (and its child widgets) paint over the dropdown. Confirmed via `document.elementFromPoint()` over an open option's center — it returns the `stSelectbox` element above it, not the option, so the option never receives the click.

Workaround (lifts the dropdown above the dialog):

```python
st.markdown(
    "<style>[data-testid='stSelectboxVirtualDropdown']{z-index:1000070!important}</style>",
    unsafe_allow_html=True,
)
```

candidate_rows.text:
## What is State?

We define access to a Streamlit app in a browser tab as a **session**. For each browser tab that connects to the Streamlit server, a new session is created. Streamlit reruns your script from top to bottom every time you interact with your app. Each reruns takes place in a blank slate: no variables are shared between runs.

Session State is a way to share variables between reruns, for each user session. In addition to the ability to store and persist state, Streamlit also exposes the ability to manipulate state using Callbacks. Session state also persists across pages inside a [multipage app](/develop/concepts/multipage-apps).

In this guide, we will illustrate the usage of **Session State** and **Callbacks** as we build a stateful Counter app.

For details on the Session State and Callbacks API, please refer to our [Session State API Reference Guide](/develop/api-reference/caching-and-state/st.session_state).

Also, check out this Session State basics tutorial video by Streamlit Developer Advocate Dr. Marisa Smith to get started:

<YouTube videoId="92jUAXBmZyU" />

candidate_rows.text:
### Trigger values: Event-based communication

**Purpose**: Signal one-time events or user interactions.

**When to use**: For user actions like clicks, form submissions, or other discrete events.

Trigger values have the following behavior:

- Are transient and only available for one script rerun.
- Reset to `None` after the rerun completes.
- Accessible via direct property access on the result object and through Session State (when mounted with a key).
- Updated using `setTriggerValue(key, value)` in JavaScript.

candidate_rows.title: dataframes
candidate_rows.text:
### Access edited data

Sometimes, it is more convenient to know which cells have been changed rather than getting the entire edited dataframe back. Streamlit makes this easy through the use of [Session State](/develop/concepts/architecture/session-state). If a `key` parameter is set, Streamlit will store any changes made to the dataframe in Session State.

This snippet shows how you can access changed data using Session State:

```python
st.data_editor(df, key="my_key", num_rows="dynamic") # 👈 Set a key
st.write("Here's the value in Session State:")
st.write(st.session_state["my_key"]) # 👈 Show the value in Session State
```

In this code snippet, the `key` parameter is set to `"my_key"`. After the data editor is created, the value associated to `"my_key"` in Session State is displayed in the app using `st.write`. This shows the additions, edits, and deletions that were made.

This can be useful when working with large dataframes and you only need to know which cells have changed, rather than access the entire edited dataframe.

Use all we've learned so far and apply them to the above embedded app. Try editing cells, adding new rows, and deleting rows.

Notice how edits to the table are reflected in Session State. When you make any edits, a rerun is triggered which sends the edits to the backend. The widget's state is a JSON object containing three properties: **edited_rows**, **added_rows**, and **deleted rows:**.

candidate_rows.title: Enhance menu button with download payload capability
candidate_rows.text:
### Why?

Today, `st.menu_button` only communicates **which option was selected** on the rerun where the user picks something; **sending bytes to the browser still requires `st.download_button`** (or other workarounds). In practice that causes:
- **Awkward UX**: pick a format from the menu, then click again to download—or rely on `st.session_state` because the menu’s return value resets on later reruns.
- **Repeated boilerplate**: every app reimplements mapping from “format label” → `data` / `file_name` / `mime`.
- **Cost vs. laziness**: precomputing every variant (e.g. large PDFs or zips) wastes CPU and memory; deferring generation until after a choice fights Streamlit’s rerun model unless authors invent their own patterns.
A combined primitive would match common product UI, reduce custom session-state hacks, and make multi-format export easier to build and maintain.

candidate_rows.title: Stucked Hover in streamlit-bokeh charts
candidate_rows.text:
### Summary

When using Bokeh charts embedded in Streamlit, an issue occurs during page rerendering (triggered by widget interaction, page reload, or Streamlit state updates). If the cursor is hovering over a chart data point while the rerender is in progress and a Bokeh hover tooltip is visible, the tooltip remains rendered on the screen after the rerender completes.

The hover overlay becomes detached from the chart lifecycle and persists across page transitions. The artifact remains visible even when navigating to different Streamlit pages.

The issue disappears only after performing a full browser hard refresh (Ctrl + F5 / Ctrl + Shift + R).
